preamble: Rounding and raising of a long nasalized low vowel [ã(ː)] to oral [o(ː)], with loss of nasality. The best-documented case is in the Ingvaeonic (North Sea Germanic) languages: long nasal *ą̄, from Proto-Germanic *-anh- and from the Ingvaeonic nasal spirant law (*-ns-, *-nþ-), became ō in Old English and Old Frisian, and in part of Old Saxon. Because the nasal vowel was not fronted by Anglo-Frisian brightening, it stayed distinct from oral *ā, which became ǣ. The change explains English goose, tooth, other and brought beside German Gans, Zahn, ander and the n of bringen.

examples.note: Nasal spirant law gave long nasal *ą̄, which was raised and rounded to ō; Modern English goose.
Modern English tooth; German Zahn keeps the nasal.
Here the nasal vowel goes back to the older Proto-Germanic loss of n before h.
North Frisian tôs, toss continue the ō.
Variant forms āthar, andar show that the rounding was not general in Old Saxon.
Attested beside tand, with the nasal consonant restored.
